name: Narrowneck Reef (Gold Coast Reef)
year: Construction began August 1999, completed by December 2000 [R2][R8]; renewed/topped up with 84 more containers June 2018 [R2][R9][R14]. [Added 2026-10-10] Blacka et al. (2013, p.94) also give construction from August 1999, main phase complete December 2000, with crest raise/trim work in 2001, 2002, 2004 and 2006 and about 50 further containers 2001-2007 (p.97) [R23].
type: Submerged multi-purpose artificial reef (MPR) built from sand-filled geotextile containers ("mega sandbags"), placed on the seabed by split-hull barge with GPS positioning [R1][R2][R3][R9].
purpose: Primary: coastal/erosion protection for the Narrowneck isthmus, where only ~100 m of land separates the Nerang River from the ocean [R2][R14]. Secondary ("multi-purpose"): surfing amenity, folded in partly for public-relations value in a surf-centric region [R2]. A tertiary, unplanned outcome was ecological habitat creation [R1][R3][R8][R9].
size: Volume approx. 70,000 m3 of sand (the largest multi-purpose reef ever built at the time), from approx. 400 geotextile containers each approx. 20 m long, 3-4.5 m diameter [R1][R9][R3]. Footprint reported as 350 m x 600 m, split "V" shape, 200 m offshore, bags 1-10 m below sea level [R9]; a second source directly states the reef "measures 450 meters long by 250 meters wide" [R8] -- the two footprint figures disagree and both are given per the reference rule. Crest lowered 1 m before construction, landing about 1.5 m below the low-tide waterline [R2][R3]; by 2017 low-tide depth over the reef measured 2.5-2.6 m, i.e. the crest had sunk/settled deeper than designed [R2]. [Added 2026-10-10] SOURCES DISAGREE on footprint: Blacka et al. (2013, Table 4.2 p.65) give a V-shape of 170 m longshore x 280 m cross-shore (maximum dimensions), water depth 2-10 m, offshore 100-600 m, min. submergence 1.0 m [R23] - a third figure beside 350 x 600 m [R9] and 450 x 250 m [R8]; all three kept, unresolved. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.2) also quote about 70,000 m3 (Jackson 2007) [R22]. For comparison the 3D model work (2026-10-10) counts 534 containers x 147 m3 = 78,500 m3 placed, of which only 17-27 % remains as an exposed mound [R24]. SOURCES DISAGREE on crest lowering: the card's '1 m' [R2][R3] vs Blacka (p.94) design -1.0 m AHD to built -1.5 m AHD, i.e. 0.5 m [R23]; the 3D work measures the present crest at -2.2 m AHD [R24] (see as_built_vs_design). Container counts and volume in the primary monitoring papers (2026-10-10 audit): 408 containers, 20 m long, 3-4.5 m diameter, placed August 1999 - December 2000 (Jackson et al. 2007, printed p.4); about 450 by 2006 (+10 in 2002-03, +15 in 2004, +17 in 2006; Jackson et al. 2012, p.3 and Fig 4 table p.4); +84 in the 2017-18 renewal [R26][R27][R25]; about 534 placed in total. The project's 147 m3 per container is DERIVED: 60,000 m3 (Jackson et al. 2007, Table 2, printed p.13, Narrowneck column [R26]) / 408 containers (same paper, p.4), this project, 07_scale/shapes/narrowneck-gold-coast/HANDOFF.md section 3c and 3d/METHODS_3D.md assumption A12 (the same 147 m3 is assumed for the later containers). So the 70,000 m3 quoted by the card's sources and the 60,000 m3 behind it are not reconciled here. Project-traced footprint (not a source statement): the visible container field on the Esri image of 8 Aug 2020 covers 6,239 m2 (arms 5,948 m2; bounding box 113.3 x 157.4 m; a lower bound, the deeper toe is not visible); the council asset polygon (OBJECTID 4637) is 171 x 262 m, 34,565 m2, which agrees with Blacka's 170 x 280 m [R23][R28]; the card's 350 x 600 m [R9] and 450 x 250 m [R8] are not supported by either.
cost: Original 1999 build: AUD $2.3 million (approx. AUD $30/m3) per one source [R3], and separately "roughly $2.1 million AUD... over the first 10 years" per another [R5] -- both given since they disagree on scope (one-off build vs. 10-year total). Lior's own notes and a Hebrew-language source both give "$2.5 million," currency unspecified [R19][R20] -- not reconciled with the figures above. 2017-2018 renewal: approx. AUD $2 million per Mayor Tom Tate, as reported by the Gold Coast Bulletin via The Inertia [R10]. [Added 2026-10-10] Blacka et al. (2013, A.2.7 p.101, Table 4.4 p.69): total A$2.8 M including top-ups and maintenance (Jackson & Corbett 2007) = about A$3.9 M in 2013 AUD, A$56 per m3 (not comparable with the card's A$30/m3, a different basis and year); about two thirds construction, one third studies (Ranasinghe 2001); A$9,800 minimum per metre of beach protected [R23]. Economic context (p.100): a 25-year ARI erosion event about A$305 M (1996 AUD), 5-year ARI about A$47 M, Gold Coast surf industry about A$160 M per year [R23].
cost_usd_approx: Very rough conversions by this report (not sourced): original build AUD $2.3M (1999 AUD~USD 0.65) approx. USD $1.5M; 2017-2018 renewal AUD $2M (2018 AUD~USD 0.75) approx. USD $1.5M. ASSUMPTION: the exchange rates (AUD/USD 0.65 for 1999, 0.75 for 2018) are unsourced estimates of this project; order of magnitude only.
financed_by: Gold Coast City Council, as part of its Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R1][R2][R9][R13]. No private or state/federal co-funding was found in any of the sources listed in References (a negative search result of this card, not a sourced statement).
motivation: Erosion problem predates the reef by decades: a 1971 Delft University of Technology report, commissioned by the Queensland Government, recommended a groyne at Narrowneck [R9][R13]. Training walls built at the Spit in 1985 helped erosion further north but not at Narrowneck itself, and Cyclone Nancy (1990) eroded the beach back to the boulder wall protecting the Nerang River [R2]. Gold Coast City Council chose an artificial reef instead of the recommended groyne, branding it a "Multi-Purpose Reef" so that surfing amenity could be folded into the PR case in a surf-centric city [R2][R9][R13]. No evidence found of state/federal political involvement or a single named political champion for the original 1999 project; Mayor Tom Tate became the public face of the 2017-2018 renewal [R10]. [Added 2026-10-10] Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4): the decision to build was driven by a cost-benefit analysis (Raybould and Mules 1998), as part of the Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy (Queensland Environment Award 2000); the first MPR designed primarily for coastal protection with surfing secondary (p.2) [R22].
designer: Original 1999 design: Prof. Kerry Black and Shaw Mead (University of Waikato, NZ; later founders of coastal-engineering firm ASR) [R11]. ICM (International Coastal Management, Gold Coast) separately credits its founder Angus Jackson with leading the project as part of the wider Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R3] -- the two attributions disagree on lead designer; both given. The 2017-2018 renewal's coastal-engineering consultant was reported by Swellnet as ICM [R2].
contractor: Not named for the 1999 build beyond "Gold Coast City Council" as project owner [R2][R9]. For the 2017-2018 renewal, the placement barge was the split-hull dredger Faucon, whose skipper gave on-record comments to Swellnet [R2].
status_now: Still in place and monitored by Gold Coast City Council as of the most recent sources found (2019 monitoring, 2026 commentary) [R12][R14]. As of January 2026, the Gold Coast mayor announced plans to "fast-track" a separate, new rockwall/groyne structure immediately south of Narrowneck -- not a rebuild of the existing reef -- contested by local surfer/environmental group Save Our Spit Alliance; a live, unresolved controversy, not a completed project [R12].
hover_text: A 70,000 m3 sand-filled geotextile reef built 1999-2000 for about AUD $2.3M to protect Narrowneck's isthmus; it worked well for coastal protection but a last-minute 1-metre crest-lowering decision left the promised surf underperforming, while the reef became an unplanned ecological hotspot whose fishing traffic then tore the bags with boat anchors, forcing a 2017-2018 renewal [R1][R2][R3][R9][R11].
design_as_planned: Designed by Kerry Black (University of Waikato) and Shaw Mead, using refraction-diffraction (WBEND) and Boussinesq wave modelling, checked against a 1:50-scale physical model at the UNSW Water Research Laboratory [R5][R11]. Stated targets: widen the beach 20-30 m in the reef's lee and produce surfable waves under defined conditions [R5]. A 2007 performance report (cited by Swellnet) noted the reef needed "long period, clean swell" to replicate the modelled wave shape, and that "larger swells, lower tides, and offshore winds have the potential to produce hollow, plunging breakers" [R2] -- the promised surf was explicitly conditional. The original design was a split "V" shape for both left- and right-hand rides with a paddling channel between the arms [R3][R9]. [Added 2026-10-10] Design criteria (Blacka et al. 2013, A.2.1-A.2.4 p.94-96): the aim was for over 80% (about 420,000 of 500,000 m3/yr) of the northward longshore drift to bypass; the empirical method predicted an 80 m salient, GENESIS needed a 30% wave-height reduction for a 50 m shoreline shift, and the WRL physical model gave wave transmission 0.5 over the crest and 0.9 at the shoreline, i.e. a 30-40 m salient at most; all design studies used the original -1.0 m AHD crest [R23]. Site: Hs about 1.0 m, tide range 2 m, beach slope 1:50 [R23]. Surf design basis: Burleigh Heads and Kirra surfing parameters (Mead 2000); headlands of several million m3 cannot be replicated (Mead & Borrero 2011, p.2-3) [R22].
as_built_vs_design: The most consequential change was a late, last-minute council decision to lower the reef's crest by 1 metre before construction -- "the change would have no effect on sand accretion but was terminal to Narrowneck becoming a good surfing reef," per Swellnet [R2]. Otherwise the built reef followed the approx. 400-container, approx. 70,000 m3 design, placed via split-hull barge with GPS [R1][R3][R9]. By approx. 2011 an underwater survey found several containers missing or damaged and seaward containers buried by sand [R4]. By 2017 the bags had "settled further into the sand" over 17 years, deeper than as-built [R2]. Designer Shaw Mead later attributed geotextile-bag failures across his firm's projects worldwide to specific causes per site, identifying boat anchors as the Gold Coast failure mechanism: "The containers failed due to a number of reasons including anchors (Gold Coast), debris strikes (Kovalam), during construction with over-filling (Mount Reef), propellor strike (Boscombe)" [R11]. [Added 2026-10-10] SOURCES DISAGREE on the crest lowering: Blacka et al. (2013, A.2.1 p.94) state the original design crest was -1.0 m AHD and that Gold Coast City Council and ICM adopted a lower -1.5 m AHD crest for safety, with possible top-up, i.e. a 0.5 m lowering; all design modelling used -1.0 m (A.2.2 p.95) [R23]. The card's Swellnet figure of 1 m [R2] is kept as the conflicting source. The crest was later not topped up after settling, to keep user risk manageable, which Blacka thinks contributed to the poor protection performance (Section 5.2 p.77-78; Fig 5.1 shows the reef 'sucking dry' in a wave trough) [R23]. Crest raised or trimmed in 2001, 2002, 2004 and 2006, about 50 more containers placed 2001-2007, peak placement 90-100 containers per month (p.94, 97) [R23]. Containers stable in 8-10 m maximum waves; nine storms with H>5 m by 2002; a composite geotextile was added to later bags after damage by anchors, spears, knives and boards (p.98) [R23]. Mead & Borrero (2011, p.3): the split-hull dredge could not position the filled containers exactly, so the structure is non-uniform, which reduced surfability [R22]. 3D work 2026-10-10: measured present crest -2.2 m AHD (Vieira da Silva 2021), 0.7 m deeper than the -1.5 m built crest; 17-27 % of the 78,500 m3 placed stands as an exposed mound, the rest buried, stacked, displaced or lost [R24]. Crest levels by source (all are statements, not agreed): design -0.67 m AHD (Black & Mead 2001, as quoted by Vieira da Silva et al. 2021 [R29]; the 2001 paper itself was not opened) and Waikato model -1.0 m AHD (Jackson et al. 2007); adopted for the 1999 contract -1.5 m AHD (-0.5 m LAT); target crest -1.5 m LAT = RL -2.5 m AHD ('compromise between safety and surfing') (Jackson et al. 2007, printed pp.4, 7) [R26]; measured after the 2018 top-up -2.2 m AHD (Vieira da Silva et al. 2021, accepted manuscript p.5) [R29]. AHD = LAT + 0.760 m at the Gold Coast Seaway (MSQ 2014), so -2.2 m AHD = 1.44 m below LAT [R25]. The card's '1.5 m below the low-tide waterline' matches the -1.5 m LAT target only (DERIVED: comparison of the Swellnet/ICM wording [R2][R3] with the target level in Jackson et al. 2007 p.7 [R26]).
outcome: Coastal protection: judged successful by the council and most independent sources; an 11-year monitoring study (Jackson et al., ICCE proceedings) found 2009 storm erosion "was accommodated within the wider beach created in 1999," with gradual post-storm recovery producing a mild groyne effect [R4]. A 2019 City statement described continued sand-volume increases, but specifically in offshore sandbars rather than the upper beach -- contradicting earlier (2010-era) reports of a 30-50 m salient, which Google Earth historical imagery does not corroborate [R14]. Wikipedia (citing Turner 2006) gives an independently monitored beach-widening figure of approx. 20 m, lower than the 30-50 m figure elsewhere [R1][R14]; both given per the reference rule. Surfing: consistently underperforming versus expectations -- "disappointing in its secondary objective to improve surfing" [R9]; surfers "seldom surf the reef," persisting after the 2017-2018 renewal [R14]. An earlier study (via ecoshape.org) reported the reef broke waves "roughly 50% of the time," faces 0.7-2.0 m, average ride 150-200 m / 30 s, "fun, but not hollow, in average conditions" [R5]. Ecology: widely reported as an unplanned success -- popular fishing/diving/snorkelling site with macro-algae, fish and reported turtle activity on the geotextile substrate [R1][R3][R8][R9]; the 2011 survey found "high abundance and biodiversity" despite sand-burial and container damage [R4]. [Added 2026-10-10] SOURCES DISAGREE on the salient: Mead & Borrero (2011, p.4, Fig. 5 p.5) report ARGUS monitoring (Blacka et al. 2008) with beach widening of 30-50 m in the lee over about 2 km after 12 years, the chart annotated 'salient widths 50-100 m' [R22]. Blacka et al. (2013, p.98-100) argue the published 20-50 m salient is a likely misreading: WRL beach widths were measured against an arbitrary dune reference line that dips away from the coast near the reef (p.98) [R23]. Turner (2005) found about 20 m accretion within 1000 m of the reef in 2001-2003; Blacka et al. (2008) found over 8 years the shoreline receded 2.8 m/yr north and south and 4.3 m/yr in the lee, ending about 15 m further back than its neighbours by mid-2008 (planform perturbation only about 10 m by eye; Figs A.7, A.8); a 1.5 million m3 nourishment south of the reef earlier complicates the analysis [R23]. Surfing: rides up to 60 s from the reef onto adjacent sandbars (Corbett 2010a, via Mead & Borrero p.3), below expectations [R22]. Blacka rates both coastal protection and surfing 'Minor' (Table 4.1 p.63), and notes the design models over-predicted the salient (Black & Andrews 2001, p.25) [R23].
why_worked_or_failed: Coastal protection worked primarily because the reef's core hydraulic function -- dissipating wave energy offshore and trapping sediment in the nearshore sandbar system -- does not depend on precise crest depth or bag integrity to the same degree surf-wave shaping does; even a degraded, buried or partially damaged reef still perturbs the sand-transport regime [R4][R14]. Surfing underperformed for a documented, specific reason: the council's last-minute 1-metre crest-lowering decision, made for reasons unrelated to surf quality, put the structure too deep for consistent wave-breaking under normal swell/tide/wind combinations [R2]. Compounding this, geotextile bags are inherently fragile: Shaw Mead stated that losing even a single sand-filled container changes the seabed shape and degrades wave quality, and that Gold Coast's containers specifically failed due to boat anchors [R11]. Mead's broader verdict: he "no longer believes in the viability of geotextile bags for artificial reef construction," having led a critical industry review approximately a decade after Narrowneck "which led to the change to traditional rock construction methods of the most recent MPRs built" [R11]. [Added 2026-10-10] The modelled long-period clean swell needed to reproduce the predicted salient is unlike typical, shorter-period Gold Coast waves (Blacka et al. 2013, p.96, 100); the crest was not topped up after settling (p.77-78) [R23]. The reef cannot reproduce headland sheltering, and its non-uniform container placement reduced surfability (Mead & Borrero 2011, p.2-3) [R22].
unexpected_results: Ecological colonisation and the resulting fishing/anchor-damage cycle: the reef's unplanned success as a fish habitat drew recreational fishing traffic, whose boat anchors are identified as the specific mechanism that tore the geotextile containers [R11] -- an ecological win directly causing the structural failure that required the 2017-2018 renewal. "Moving the goalposts" on beach-widening claims: early (2010-era) monitoring described a clear 30-50 m salient; by 2019 the City's official position shifted to say a salient was "never expected" and sand build-up was always meant to be offshore -- flagged by multiple Swellnet commenters as inconsistent with what residents were originally told [R14]. A 2026 political sequel: 27 years after Narrowneck was built to avoid a conventional groyne, the Gold Coast mayor proposed fast-tracking a new rockwall/groyne immediately adjacent to it, prompting the same updrift/downdrift erosion-displacement objections coastal engineers raise about hard groynes generally [R12]. Depth-measurement uncertainty: the City's post-renewal survey data claims no settlement of the new containers, directly contradicting anecdotal local reports that the new bags were already breaking less often and appeared to be settling [R14].
could_be_better: Experts'/engineers' view: Shaw Mead, the reef's original designer, has publicly stated (in a critical review conducted roughly a decade after Narrowneck was built) that sand-filled geotextile containers should not be used for multi-purpose reef construction at all, and that the industry has since moved to rock construction [R11]. Swellnet's 2017 reporting singles out the crest-lowering decision as the single design change most responsible for the surf underperformance, implying a purely surf-focused crest depth would have produced a better wave without necessarily compromising protection [R2]. Surfers'/locals' view: commenters were blunter -- one ("warddy," 2019) called it an "absolute waste of money" and suggested rock construction instead; another ("the-spleen_2") noted "beach widening" had originally been "the core of the project" as pitched by Griffith University, and found it "funny to see how the idea has changed over time" toward the offshore-sandbar framing [R14].
relevance_to_israel: Narrowneck's central lesson for a Haifa or other Israeli Mediterranean project is the crest-depth-versus-tide-range trade-off: the reef's surf underperformance is traced by an independent source specifically to a council decision to change crest depth relative to the tide datum, made for reasons unrelated to surfing, which then dominated wave-breaking outcomes [R2]. The Gold Coast has a meaningful astronomical tide range (crest explicitly set "1.5 m below the low tide waterline") [R2][R3] -- a variable a designer must actively engineer around, since a fixed crest depth performs differently at high versus low tide. Lior's own draft outreach material argues the Mediterranean's smaller tidal range at Haifa is an advantage for reef stability and maintenance ("the tide conditions here allow high stability and natural long-term maintenance") [R18] -- this is Lior's own hypothesis, not an independently sourced engineering conclusion, and no numeric Haifa/Mediterranean tide-range figure was found in the sources fetched for this dossier. If correct (INFERENCE of this card's author from Lior's hypothesis [R18]; no Haifa tide-range figure is sourced here, so this is unsourced), a Haifa reef would face a smaller version of Narrowneck's tide-datum problem, making crest-depth choice a one-time design decision rather than a chronic multi-condition compromise. Separately, Narrowneck's identified failure mechanism -- boat anchors tearing geotextile bags that had become a popular fishing spot [R11] -- is directly transferable: any Israeli geotextile-based reef that succeeds ecologically should expect the same anchor-damage risk and may want to restrict anchoring or use more anchor-resistant materials such as rock, per Mead's own post-Narrowneck design shift [R11]. Gold Coast tide planes for comparison (Seaway, MSQ 2026, above LAT): MHWS 1.53, MLWS 0.22, HAT 2.03 m, so a spring range of 1.31 m [R25]. A Haifa figure is still not sourced in this card.

reviews.quote_or_summary: "I personally can't remember too many, if any, good days on the reef itself which was a major let down after the anticipation built up. I do remember that it did sort of break up the banks inside it both to the north and south which did on occasion deliver good waves." [R2]
"Cool. A long time ago I had a fun surf out there. Any improvement is a plus." [R2]

"Absolute waste of money ... When will these clowns realise just drop some rocks in a triangular shape and whamo pick a peak and dissipate the sand surge at the same time plus create a fisherie." [R14]
"Because that would be too easy and wouldn't justify the jobs of the 'experts' who created this abomination." [R14]

"I used to surf up that end a lot, including Naz, and never noticed a salient. A friend of a friend was in the original Griffith pitch and 'beach widening' was the core of the project so it's funny to see how the idea has changed over time." [R14]
Describes Cyclone Oma's February 2019 erosion at Narrowneck as the "worst erosion at Narrowneck... worst in 40 yrs." [R14]

videos.title: NARROWNECK REEF
videos.what_it_shows: Interview-style documentary with the reef's design engineer explaining why Narrowneck Reef was built (Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy, 1999), how the geotextile sandbags were placed by split-hull dredge, why a submerged reef beat groynes/beach dewatering, and the marine growth/monitoring outcomes over approx. 10 years.
key_quotes: [00:00:19] "The [Narrowneck] Reef is a geotextile bag reef and its primary objective was Coastal protection."

[00:01:00] "...what we wanted was another control point just this side of Surfers Paradise we looked at groins we looked at beach dewatering... and the one that came out best was a submerged artificial Reef without the added bonuses of Surfing and Diving it was clearly the best solution."
[00:01:33] "We've constructed a structure that you can't see but it's constantly reducing the sand transport and the storm cut so we have a wider Beach a more stable Beach."

[00:02:52] "The difference between a geotextile structure and a concrete or rock structure is the type of growth we get... 10 m of water we're getting Kelps we're getting Turtles and I've dive with dolphins."

verdict_reason: Verdict 'mixed' was assigned by the research agent that wrote this card (verified_on 2026-09-24, enriched 2026-10-10), not by Lior; no Lior ruling on it is recorded. Basis: the structure survives after more than 25 years and was renewed in 2018 [R2][R9][R14], and an independent monitoring record exists [R4][R7]; but the surf function is weak (crest changed for safety, surfing use declined) [R2][R5], the shoreline salient is disputed (20-50 m claimed vs a likely misreading, Blacka p.98-100 [R23]) and bags were damaged by anchors [R11][R14]. Re-checked 2026-10-10; unchanged.
